node.label: Cole Harris
node.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
node.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Cole Harris (R. Cole Harris, 1936–2022); The Seigneurial System in Early Canada (1966); 'Theory and Synthesis in Historical Geography' (Canadian Geographer, 1971); 'The Simplification of Europe Overseas' (Annals of the AAG, 1977); 'The Historical Mind and the Practice of Geography' (1978); ed., with Geoffrey J. Matthews as cartographer and designer, Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1: From the Beginning to 1800 (1987); 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG, 1991); The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (1997; two chapters with Robert Galois and David Demeritt); 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies, 1997/98); Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (2002); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' (BC Studies forum, 2003, with commentaries by Jo-Anne Fiske and Gordon Gibson and his reply); 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire' (Annals of the AAG, 2004); A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (2020). Readings: MacDonald (1990); Loo (1998); Clayton (2003); Fiske (2003); Napoleon (2004); Perry (2016, later reading).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14 in open copies. His own words, read: 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997/98, pp. 45–82; pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82 read closely, the rest skimmed); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' with Fiske's and Gibson's commentaries and his reply (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 137–163, read in full); the abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), read in the publisher's abstract as recorded by OpenAlex (the article body is closed and unread); the preface of the Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (1987), known only through MacDonald's quotations. Reception read in full: Graham A. MacDonald on the Atlas (Manitoba History 20, 1990, web text); Tina Loo on The Resettlement of British Columbia (BC Studies 117, 1998, pp. 64–67); Daniel Clayton's guest editorial on Making Native Space (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 5–11); Val Napoleon on Making Native Space (BC Studies 141, 2004, pp. 114–118). Later reading: Perry's 2016 reply in the BC Studies forum on her Colonial Relations (p. 112). Unread: the books themselves (The Seigneurial System, the Atlas, The Resettlement of British Columbia, Making Native Space, A Bounded Land), the 1977 and 1991 Annals essays (known through Clayton's note), the 1994 Ethnohistory article on smallpox, the Canadian Geographer review symposium on Making Native Space (2003; known through Napoleon's summary), and the Native Studies Review forum 'Appraising Cole Harris' Making Native Space' (16:2, 2005; the copy on the University of Saskatchewan site returned 404). He is not presented as a founder of historical geography or of settler-colonial history: the Atlas was a collective work with a cartographer and many contributors, and the texts read do not cite Wolfe. Contested in period by Loo (1998) and Napoleon (2004) on Native voices and agency, by Fiske (2003) on the symbolic, and by the Canadian Geographer symposium (2003, as Napoleon summarises it). Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

proposed_edges.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: they cite Merivale, Kymlicka and Macklem, not Wolfe, and the books are unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Harris wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later reading, labelled: Perry (BC Studies 190, 2016, p. 112) says her 2001 book read British Columbia 'within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. A Bounded Land (2020), with its 'Postscript: The Boundaries of Settler Colonialism', is cited at title level only.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The strand ('Harris explains reserve-making as geographical dispossession, backed by state power, capital and settlers') already lists him and these works.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colonialism read through its geographies: the land system as a 'spatial discipline' that bounded Native movement, and the reserve line as the 'primal line on the land' of British Columbia (1997–2003), which Clayton (2003) offered as a model of 'colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 2003 forum précis (p. 138, read): 'From a Native perspective, an even more enveloping discipline may have been imposed by an introduced land system and its associated settlement geography, which, by controlling where they could and could not go, increasingly bounded and channeled their movements.' The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) is unread; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) quotes it: the land system '[imposing] a spatial discipline with a profound capacity to modify Native life' (p. 101), and by 1881 'Native power over the Lower Mainland and, to a considerable extent, earlier Native lifeworlds had collapsed' (p. 102); Loo: 'According to Harris, in British Columbia disciplinary power rested on the land system (Chapters 3 and 4). To me, this is the heart of Harris's argument … the links between colonization and geographical change are most visible' (p. 65). Making Native Space (2002) is unread; Clayton (2003, read) quotes Harris's aim to tell 'the colonial construction of space in British Columbia' (p. 6, citing pp. xxi, xxviii) and his view that the reserve line 'became, in a sense, the primal line on the land of British Columbia, the one that facilitated or constrained all others' (p. 7); Napoleon (2004, p. 116, read) quotes the reserves 'displayed rather like insects on pins' (p. 271) and their 'fixed place in the Cartesian space of the survey system and in the minds of officials and settlers'. Disciplinary reception (Clayton, a geographer who began working with Harris as a UBC graduate student, p. 6): Harris is 'very much the historian's geographer' (p. 5); the book 'will be more widely read and appreciated for what it says about the spatiality of colonialism, or what Harris sees as colonialism's "geographical core" (xxiv)' (p. 7); he offers '(however unwittingly) a powerful and important programme for a postcolonial historical geography that significantly departs from current critical norms' (p. 7), 'a timely and potent model for the critical appreciation of colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire' (p. 11), Clayton's contrast with work that 'fixates on the formal disciplinary links between geography and empire' (p. 7). Qualifications: Clayton thinks Harris 'insulate[s]' his historical geography 'from some potentially fruitful comparative lines of inquiry and a fuller digging into theory' (p. 9); the existing spatialhistory row records that the analysis of Merivale and imperial policy 'is not Indigenous testimony'. Distinct from edge 1, which carries the explanation of dispossession in the settler-colonial field; this edge carries the spatial method as historical geography. Compare edge_693 (post → geography, Said in Driver's 'geography's empire').
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The Making Native Space strand already lists him; its focus (colonial land policies as spatial arrangements) is the intervention.

proposed_edges.relationship: Editor of the Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (1987), a collaborative atlas of sixty-nine plates from the first human occupation to about 1800 that, in his preface, emphasised 'the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life' over geopolitical events, aimed to 'accord full place to native peoples' and judged that it had not done so, and placed early Canada in Innis's staple trades
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The Atlas is unread. His preface is known through Graham A. MacDonald's review (Manitoba History 20, Autumn 1990, web text read in full; no page numbers), which quotes it: 'At least some of our biases are intentional. We have sought to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases: geo-political events and their territorial consequences'; the editors wished to 'give more attention to Atlantic Canada and to the West than is common in most interpretations of early Canada'; they tried to 'accord full place to native peoples', but for want of data the editor concludes 'we have not succeeded in doing so'; 'an atlas may lead research in some ways, but more commonly it must follow, reflecting the literature in which it is situated'; and 'As Innis maintained, the pattern of Canada has been taking shape for almost 500 years … The early Canadian economy was dominated by staple trades in fish and furs that were dependent on long-distance transportation … The country's southern boundary is not a geographical absurdity.' MacDonald's own judgements: the volume is 'a tribute to the efforts of many individuals', including students of Andrew Hill Clark such as Harris; 'There is far too much in this masterly production to reduce it to a single thesis'; the prehistory plates are the most likely to date, since the Atlas does little to acknowledge 'the mounting number of attacks' on models such as the 'ice free corridor'; most of it 'will set the standard for many years'. Other in-period witnesses: Loo (1998, p. 64, read) names 'his work on the Historical Atlas of Canada' with his two books as 'testimony to Harris's distinguished scholarly career'; Clayton (2003, p. 5, read): 'perhaps best known to Canadians for his editorship of the Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1: From the beginning to 1800 (1987)', which won the 1988 Macdonald Prize (n. 2). A contribution, not a sole authorship: Geoffrey J. Matthews was cartographer and designer, and the plates had many authors. Optional: the same endpoints as edge 2 (one new 'repeated endpoint/type' validator warning); it can be merged into edge 2 if the editor prefers one arrow.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No strand fits exactly: documentary_geographies (Darby, reconstructing geography from historical records) is the nearest; historical_gis is Olson's and Gregory's. A strand list addition is not proposed because the Atlas is unread.
proposed_edges.include_note: Not released (1.140): same endpoints and type as pe139_harris_rel_02; the Historical Atlas of Canada vol. 1 (1987) stays in the representative works.

proposed_edges.relationship: The 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era British Columbia, as anthropologists and Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977) held it, questioned: it 'needs to be approached very cautiously', since epidemics, violence and depopulation accompanied the fur trade's wealth (1997–98)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia', BC Studies 115/116 (1997/98), pp. 45–82, read at pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82. The position: Fisher, influenced by Wilson Duff's view that the fur trade 'did not destabilize Native life' and by 'his own sharp reaction to the effacement of Native peoples implicit in the "fatal impact" approach', wrote 'a remarkable and influential book — Contact and Conflict — [arguing] that Europeans and Natives met as equals on the Northwest Coast, that contact violence has been considerably exaggerated, and that an infusion of wealth created a brief high point in Northwest Coast culture' (pp. 46–47); 'Fisher's conclusions summarized and extended the prevailing anthropological understanding of the previous generation — a set of assumptions often loosely labelled the cultural enrichment hypothesis, after a phrase first used by Joyce Wike' (p. 47); 'now, twenty years later, new information is available, Native voices have repoliticized issues of land and colonial appropriation, and the intellectual climate has changed' (p. 47). The critique: 'the cultural enrichment hypothesis needs to be approached very cautiously. Crudely applied, it quickly becomes Eurocentric and far too simple. It tends to measure cultural achievement against quantitative and materialistic Western values of accumulation' (p. 80); 'There was no one culture and no fixed datum plane against which to measure cultural enrichment'; 'the enrichment hypothesis ignores too much of what was going on along the Northwest Coast during the contact years. Against enrichment measured by poles, feast goods, and the enhanced authority of some chiefs were epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (p. 81). Fur-trade power: traders' 'politics of fear — "respect" or "terror" were the traders' common words' (p. 58). Qualifications kept: 'There is good evidence for all of these developments' (p. 80); 'Native people were anything but passive victims of these new circumstances, some of which they had largely made themselves. They drew hard trading bargains' (p. 81); and he calls Fisher's book 'remarkable and influential'. The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997, unread) makes the same case in its first chapters; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) summarises the Hudson's Bay Company as a 'proto-colonial presence' (p. 34) whose rule, 'though founded on fear and violence, relied on symbolic gesture and theatre'. Clayton (2003, p. 6, read) measures Making Native Space against Contact and Conflict. No reply by Fisher was checked. Scope: a critique of one interpretation of early contact, not of the native–newcomer field or of agency-centred work as such; edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques of the field's framing.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Fisher sits in native_newcomer/indigenous_actors_in_trade, which also holds Ray (Indians in the Fur Trade, 1974), whom the critique does not name; the strand address would be broader than the critique, so none is set.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colonial-discourse studies criticised for an emphasis on culture that 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'; he proposed explaining 'colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized' instead, while allowing that 'several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights' (2004)
proposed_edges.map_label: Harris: culture overweighted in colonial-discourse studies, 2003–04
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. Abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94:1 (2004), pp. 165–182 (publisher's abstract, read via OpenAlex; article body closed and unread): 'The emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism tends to obscure other forms of colonial power while making it impossible to contextualize the cultural argument and assess its salience. Rather than focusing on texts, systems of signification, and procedures of knowledge generation, as the colonial discourse literature is wont to do, a fuller understanding of colonial powers is achieved by explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized. In so doing, the issue of power is not prejudged'; it ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' The 2003 précis (BC Studies, pp. 137–138, read) gives culture one of four roles, the legitimation of dispossession. Qualifications: he uses the literature he criticises. In 1997–98 (p. 59 n. 39, read) he cites Said's Orientalism as 'The original and most influential discussion' of the European categories of civilized and savage; Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) finds Making Native Space 'Informed by Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Michel Foucault, and E.P. Thompson'. Clayton's reading, labelled as his (2003, read): Harris is 'neither a close student of the imperial imagination nor a slavish follower of the powerful postcolonial theories' (p. 8, Clayton's paraphrase); his findings fuel 'his suspicion of an international postcolonial literature that, in his view, tends to overplay the hands of culture and discourse relative to other forms of power' (pp. 8–9, citing the 2004 essay as forthcoming); yet he 'favours (again however unwittingly) a certain postcolonial narrative' (p. 9) and 'has absorbed a body of ideas about the ascriptive power of colonial discourse … that were initially advanced by Said' (p. 10). No reply from a postcolonial critic was checked.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The critique names 'the colonial discourse literature' as a whole, not one strand. The nearest strand is post/imperial_knowledge (Said), which he also draws on; an edge to edward_said was considered and not proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foucault's sovereign and disciplinary power as Harris's terms for the fur traders' 'politics of fear' and for the colonial land system and its 'disciplinary technologies' (1997–2004), used selectively
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, p. 58, read): the traders' retaliations 'in public theatres of power' were 'what Michel Foucault called sovereign power, a sporadic, local, and highly visible seizure of property or life', quoting Discipline and Punish (n. 37); he adds that 'In the Cordillera, such power did not validate a discourse of legal rights and property relations, as it did in Europe.' 2003 précis (p. 138, read) and 2004 abstract: the management of dispossession by 'disciplinary technologies'. In-period readers. Loo (1998, read): the HBC's power was 'what Harris, following Michel Foucault, calls "sovereign power"', and 'the resettlement of British Columbia turned on "disciplinary power,"' which in British Columbia 'rested on the land system' (p. 65); the book 'is shaped by his reading of a diverse and complex international theoretical literature on power' (p. 64). Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) names Foucault with Fanon, Said and Thompson. Qualification: Clayton (2003, p. 9, read) reports that Harris never '"lets theory loose" in British Columbia, as he puts it (xvii)'. The 1991 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG), which Clayton lists among his methodological essays (p. 6 n. 3), is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Val Napoleon's review of Making Native Space (2004): the book 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history', its proposals needed 'contemporary Aboriginal voices', and grounding Aboriginal rights in 'difference' is problematic, since Aboriginal peoples 'still have a special place in Canada' whether or not they are 'the same as everyone else'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Val Napoleon's review (BC Studies 141, Spring 2004, pp. 114–118, read in full), not a verdict of the Indigenous history field, whose roster also lists Harris as a historian. Her criticisms: 'Harris recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history as it unfolded for roughly a century' (p. 115); Part 4, 'Land and Livelihood', is 'somewhat incongruous with the rest of the book' because there he moves from the archival record to argument (p. 117); the politics of difference is 'nonetheless problematic' (p. 117), and 'Speaking as a First Nations person, I do not believe that it matters whether Aboriginal people are the same as everyone else; we still have a special place in Canada' (p. 117); 'In my view, where historical enquiry gives way to thought about the future, Harris should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices into his discussion … It is from within the experience of this conflicted and contradictory milieu that strategies for future change must be developed and tested, not from without' (p. 117); he does not address 'the structural economic problems that small communities are encountering' (p. 115). Her praise, kept: the book gave her 'a much more textured, dynamic, and human sense of BC history' (p. 116); 'What I appreciate most … is Harris's argument that the colonial approach to land was less about legal or moral principles than about the varying self-interests of the colonizers' (p. 117); it is 'a valuable resource for both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal peoples', and she has 'recommended the book to people from several different Aboriginal communities' (p. 118). She also summarises, without quotation, the Canadian Geographer review symposium of five geographers (47:1, 2003, unread here): they suggested that Harris had '(1) appropriated the voices of patriarchy and of the colonizer' and '(5) insufficiently considered Aboriginal resistance to the reserve allocation system' (pp. 114–115), and Harris replied that 'A book … can only do so much' and 'remains unconvinced that the basic settler attitudes were gendered' (p. 115, her words). Loo (1998, p. 66, read) had made the related point that 'there are very few "Native voices"' in the 1997 book (edge 1). A field-to-person critique naming its proxy, the pattern used for quebec_historiography → fernand_ouellet.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Person entries carry no strands. On the source side no indigenous strand fits; a roster row for Napoleon is proposed instead.
proposed_edges.include_note: Released in 1.140 as a named-proxy field-to-person critique (release/fixes-1.140.md, finding 11).

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. He holds a historian row and the colonial_geography strand there, and edge_777 (spatialhistory → indigenous, comparison, 'Land and colonial geography') already carries his 1997 work at entry level with the caution that it 'does not assert adoption of his methods by Indigenous historians'. A Harris → indigenous contribution would claim more than the texts read support.

Not proposed. He has a contributor row and sits in the british_columbia strand. Loo (1998, p. 64) says the book 'exemplifies the potential of regional history', but his regional framework for Canada ('Regionalism and the Canadian Archipelago', 1982, and 'The Pattern of Early Canada', 1987) was not located or read. Lead: read those essays for an edge on Canada as an archipelago of regions.

Not proposed as a separate arrow. The only witness is MacDonald's quotation of the 1987 preface ('As Innis maintained, the pattern of Canada has been taking shape for almost 500 years …'), kept on edge 3. Revisit if the Atlas preface or The Reluctant Land is read.
Not proposed. The 2004 abstract criticises 'the colonial discourse literature' generally and does not name Said; Harris cites Said approvingly in 1997–98 (p. 59 n. 39). Edge 5 targets post.

Not proposed. Perry (2001, p. 58, read) cites Harris's 'struggle with distance' (Resettlement, ch. 6) for a point about travel, and in 2016 (p. 112) she says her 2001 book echoed 'an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. That is a later self-reading and cannot carry a dated influence. Recorded on edge 1 and in the Perry packet.
Not proposed separately. Loo's 1998 points (few Native voices; Native peoples as victims; class absent) are recorded on edge 1; Loo has a people record but no native_newcomer row.

verification.note: Read in full in the Manitoba Historical Society's web text (no page numbers). Passages used: quotations of Harris's preface on 'the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life', more attention to 'Atlantic Canada and to the West', 'accord full place to native peoples' and 'we have not succeeded in doing so', 'an atlas may lead research in some ways, but more commonly it must follow', and the Innis paragraph ('As Innis maintained, the pattern of Canada has been taking shape for almost 500 years'); MacDonald on the volume as 'a tribute to the efforts of many individuals', 'masterly production', the dating risk of the prehistory plates, and the Atlas setting 'the standard for many years'.

new_sources.title: Cole Harris, “Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia,” BC Studies 115/116 (Autumn/Winter 1997/98): 45–82.
new_sources.citation: Cole Harris, “Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia,” BC Studies 115/116 (1997/98): 45–82. doi:10.14288/bcs.v0i115/6.1723.

verification.note: Journal PDF read (https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/bcstudies/article/view/1723; OJS metadata pp. 45–82). Read closely at pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82; the sections on inscription and disease skimmed. Passages used: Fisher's Contact and Conflict as 'a remarkable and influential book' arguing 'that Europeans and Natives met as equals' (pp. 46–47); 'the cultural enrichment hypothesis, after a phrase first used by Joyce Wike' (p. 47); traders' 'politics of fear' and Foucault's 'sovereign power' (p. 58); Said's Orientalism as 'The original and most influential discussion' (p. 59 n. 39); 'the cultural enrichment hypothesis needs to be approached very cautiously' (p. 80); 'no fixed datum plane'; 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation'; 'anything but passive victims' (p. 81). An earlier version was given at the BC Studies conference, Nanaimo, May 1997 (p. 45 n. 1).

Passages used: the four sites of the power to dispossess (pp. 137–138); the land system that 'increasingly bounded and channeled their movements' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia' (p. 140); 'successful settler colonialism' (p. 144); Fiske, 'unsettling in its apparent simplicity' and the powers that 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152); Harris, 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161).

new_sources.citation: Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change, by Cole Harris, BC Studies 117 (1998): 64–67. doi:10.14288/bcs.v0i117.185301.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal PDF (https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/bcstudies/article/view/185301). Passages used: The Seigneurial System 'set the terms for the debate over the nature of New World societies in this country'; the Atlas as part of his career; colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space'; 'Work like this … exemplifies the potential of regional history'; 'international theoretical literature on power' (p. 64); 'following Michel Foucault … "sovereign power"', 'disciplinary power' resting on the land system, Harris's p. 101 'spatial discipline' and p. 102 (p. 65); 'very few "Native voices"', Native peoples 'emerge as victims', connections to colonization 'fade away' (p. 66); class not discussed; 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67).

new_sources.title: Daniel Clayton, “Guest Editorial: The Question of Making Native Space,” BC Studies 138/139 (Summer/Autumn 2003): 5–11.
new_sources.citation: Daniel Clayton, “Guest Editorial: The Question of Making Native Space,” BC Studies 138/139 (2003): 5–11. doi:10.14288/bcs.v0i138/9.1668.

verification.note: Read in full (https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/bcstudies/article/view/1668). Clayton says he began working with Harris as a UBC graduate student and that some observations stem from conversations with him (pp. 5–6 and n. 1). Passages used: 'the historian's geographer', 'best known to Canadians for his editorship of the Historical Atlas of Canada' (p. 5); methodological essays of 1971, 1978, 1991 and 'The Simplification of Europe Overseas' (1977) (p. 6 n. 3); 'arguably the most significant contribution … since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6); 'the primal line on the land' and colonialism's 'geographical core' (p. 7); 'suspicion of an international postcolonial literature' (pp. 8–9); 'lets theory loose' (p. 9); Said's 'ascriptive power of colonial discourse' (p. 10); 'colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire' (p. 11). The editorial cites the 2004 Annals essay as in press (n. 8).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period reading of Making Native Space by a historical geographer.

new_sources.citation: Val Napoleon, review of Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia, by Cole Harris, BC Studies 141 (2004): 114–118.

verification.note: Read in full in the issue's book-review PDF (OJS article 1706, pp. 105 ff.; this review pp. 114–118, page heads checked). Byline University of Victoria. Passages used: 'Informed by Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Michel Foucault, and E.P. Thompson' (p. 114); summary of the Canadian Geographer symposium (47:1, 2003) and Harris's reply (pp. 114–115); 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history'; the 'structural economic problems' of small communities (p. 115); 'a much more textured, dynamic, and human sense of BC history'; 'insects on pins' and 'Cartesian space' (p. 116); Part 4 'somewhat incongruous'; the politics of difference 'nonetheless problematic'; 'Speaking as a First Nations person …'; 'contemporary Aboriginal voices'; the colonial approach to land 'less about legal or moral principles than about the varying self-interests of the colonizers' (p. 117); 'a valuable resource for both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal peoples' (p. 118).

It names 'the colonial discourse literature', proposes 'explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized', gives the four conclusions (physical power and the state; capital and settlers; a cultural discourse of civilization and savagery; 'disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important'), and ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' row.context: Historical geographer of contact and colonialism in British Columbia; in 1997–98 he questioned the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of the fur-trade years, as anthropologists and Fisher's Contact and Conflict held it, setting against it epidemics, violence and depopulation, while calling Native people 'anything but passive victims'.
row.works: “Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia” (1997/98); The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997)
